questions.q: Why are Azure and AWS considered independent failure domains?
options: They don't share power, networking fabric, or an incident response team, so an outage in one has no mechanism to cause an outage in the other
They are independent because they are both billed in the same currency
They share the same networking fabric but different physical power sources
They are only independent if a customer pays for a premium support tier on both
questions.explain: Azure and AWS have no shared power, networking, or operational dependency, which is exactly why a regional issue on one provider does not propagate to the other.

questions.q: What happens when a service in Azure calls an AWS dependency on every request with no timeout configured, and that AWS dependency becomes slow rather than fully down?
options: Azure automatically detects the slowness and reroutes traffic without any configuration needed
Each hung call holds a connection and thread open in the Azure service, and enough of them can exhaust its capacity, making the healthy Azure service unavailable too
The calls fail instantly, so no resources are ever held open
AWS automatically cancels the Azure service's requests after a fixed internal limit
questions.explain: Without a timeout, hung calls hold connections and threads open indefinitely; enough of them exhaust the calling service's capacity, turning the dependency's degradation into an outage on the healthy side too.

questions.q: What does a circuit breaker pattern specifically accomplish in a cross-cloud call chain?
options: It permanently blocks all future calls to a dependency after a single failure
It encrypts cross-cloud traffic to prevent interception
It increases the timeout value automatically after repeated failures
After enough consecutive failures to a dependency, it stops calling that dependency for a cooldown period instead of continuing to pile up failing or hanging calls
questions.explain: A circuit breaker halts calls to a struggling dependency for a cooldown window, which is specifically what stops the cascading-failure pattern described earlier in the lesson.

questions.q: What is an example of graceful degradation as described in this lesson?
options: Retrying a failed cross-cloud call indefinitely until it eventually succeeds
Failing the entire request whenever any one dependency, however minor, is unreachable
Serving a last-known-good cached value or skipping a non-critical enrichment step when a cross-cloud dependency is unavailable, rather than failing the whole request
Shutting down the healthy cloud provider's service until the degraded one recovers
questions.explain: Graceful degradation means deciding in advance on a reduced-but-functional fallback behavior, so one unreachable dependency doesn't take down the entire response.

questions.q: How does this lesson connect its partial-failure design principle back to Lesson 17's VPN-as-failover pattern?
options: They are unrelated; Lesson 17 is about networking and this lesson is about application code only
Both are examples of the same principle at different layers: two independent paths (or providers), not either one alone, are what actually produce resilience
Both rely on the same underlying mechanism: a shared pre-shared key between gateways
Lesson 17's pattern makes this lesson's application-level patterns unnecessary
questions.explain: A VPN configured as failover for a dedicated circuit and an application built to keep functioning when one cloud provider degrades are the same resilience principle — independent paths — applied at the network layer and the application layer respectively.
